<pasted_content id="abde"> You are helping me write a specification using Spec-Driven Development (SDD). This session is ONLY for creating SPEC.md. Do NOT write code, install anything or create other files. Create exactly one file: SPEC.md. ## Project Huddle: a party-games web app for Indian friend groups. Everyone plays on their own phone; no TV/laptop is needed, but one can be used as an optional big screen. Course project; must be deployed so my professor can open it alone; built mostly autonomously by Claude Code over ~3 days. It must work reliably: the main complaint it fixes is skribbl.io resetting your score when you rejoin. ## Stack (fixed) - Next.js (App Router, TypeScript), Tailwind, Vitest, Playwright (E2E with 4-8 simulated players in parallel browser contexts), Vercel (Hobby). - Neon Postgres via DATABASE_URL, server-only. - Ably for realtime (ABLY_API_KEY server-only; clients get short-lived tokens from our server; the root key never reaches the browser). - Auth.js with Google as OPTIONAL sign-in (AUTH_SECRET, AUTH_GOOGLE_ID, AUTH_GOOGLE_SECRET). No AI APIs. - Secrets only in .env.local and Vercel; never read .env.local; never ask me to paste keys into chat. CI on GitHub Actions, ubuntu-24.04. ## Architecture rules - The server is the referee: every action goes to an API route that validates it against the game rules, saves state in Neon, and publishes the update via Ably. Game rules live in pure, unit-tested modules. - State is versioned; any client can fetch a full snapshot at any time, so missed messages and reconnects never desync a phone. - Timers are server-issued deadlines (so every phone shows the same countdown and a rejoining phone gets the correct time left). Since serverless has no background loop, deadline expiry is processed idempotently when any client reports it, so AFK players are skipped even if their phone is off. - Secret information is only ever sent to the players allowed to see it (charades movie -> actor only; imposter words per player; drawing word -> drawer only; quiz answers only after reveal). Test this by checking payloads. - Drawing strokes are batched and simplified to save data, without any visible quality loss. ## Players, rooms and crews 1. Guests join instantly with a name (any name allowed, no filter); a device token keeps their seat. Optional Google sign-in gives a permanent profile across devices; tonight's guest stats can be claimed later by signing in. 2. Rooms: join by 4-letter code, link or QR; up to 12 players. Rejoining (lock screen, refresh, Wi-Fi drop, closed tab) restores your seat and score exactly. Rooms persist for 24 hours. 3. Room creator is admin: skip a turn, kick, pause/resume, end game, undo the last scoring action, change settings between games, transfer admin. If the admin leaves or is AFK, admin passes to the longest- present player. Without any admin action, turn timers still auto-skip; after 2 missed turns a player is marked AFK and skipped (seat and score kept) until they act again. 4. Late joiners spectate and are seated at the start of the next round. 5. Game queue (e.g. Quiz -> Draw -> Charades with scoreboard breaks), rematch with the same players/teams, house rules per game (rounds, timer, points, categories, difficulty/era). 6. Teams: auto-balanced from players' past performance (explain the rating method), editable by hand. 7. Crews: a saved friend group via link; season leaderboard across game nights, per-game stats, head-to-head records, history; end-of-night awards (MVP, Best Artist, Fastest Finger, Best Imposter, Most AFK) and a shareable recap card image. 8. Gentle vibration on your turn (where the phone supports it); no sounds. 9. Demo at /demo: a room with bot players that the professor can play alone, covering every game. 10. Design: attractive modern dark theme by default plus light theme, mobile-first, large tap targets, works at 360 px, installable PWA. Big-screen mode: any laptop/TV can open the room as a display-only screen (joined by code/QR, not a player) showing the current game (question, drawing, timer, reveals) plus a live leaderboard and teams. Without a big screen, every phone has a small, always-visible leaderboard button that opens the live scores and teams at any time, without interrupting the game. ## Games (each with clear rules, scoring and timers) 1. Quiz Clash: solo or teams; speed bonus; categories Bollywood, Hollywood, cricket, India GK, world GK, science, sports; a built-in bank of at least 400 multiple-choice questions written by Claude, with automated checks (no duplicates, answer among options) and a "report question" button. 2. Dumb Charades: teams; built-in Bollywood and Hollywood movie lists (at least 200 each) by era and difficulty; only the actor sees the title; actor marks Guessed / Pass; team timer; optional steal rule. 3. Draw & Guess (skribbl-style): drawer picks 1 of 3 words; colours, sizes, eraser, undo, clear; live drawing; guesses in a chat; private "you're close!" for near-misses; letter hints over time; points by speed, drawer also scores; built-in word list (at least 500, India- aware). 4. Atlas: each place must start with the last letter of the previous one; validated against a bundled place database (countries, capitals, Indian states and cities, world cities above a population threshold, from GeoNames with attribution) with alternate spellings; used places tracked; turn timer; elimination; variants (India only, countries only); unknown places go to a quick accept vote. 5. Imposter: everyone gets the same word except the imposter (built-in word pairs, at least 150); one-word clue rounds; discussion timer; vote; reveal; the caught imposter gets one guess at the word to steal the win. 6. Most Likely To: built-in prompts (at least 150); anonymous votes; dramatic reveal. ## What SPEC.md must contain (in this order) Goal; users and main scenarios (including a hostless night, an AFK player, a phone rejoining mid-game, a night with and without a big screen); constraints; inputs/outputs (data model, message/sync protocol, timer handling); requirements R1.. in EARS form, each Must or Should (core platform, crews/rankings, the phone leaderboard button and games 1-5 are Must; big-screen mode, Most Likely To and the recap card are Should); acceptance criteria AC-1.. each pass/fail, mapped to R#, tagged Unit / E2E / Deploy / Manual, preferring Unit and E2E (with multi-player and reconnect scenarios) so Claude verifies almost everything itself; Manual checks limited to one real playtest with friends and phone install; Phase-1 deployment risks (Ably token auth from Vercel, Neon, Google sign-in, 6 real browsers in one production room, drawing throughput within Ably free limits); output files; non-goals (AI, voice/video chat, sounds, native apps, content moderation); risks with fallbacks; open questions with defaults; changelog (v0.1, today). Aim for at most ~90 requirements and ~80 ACs. When done, show me a short summary and the open questions. </pasted_content id="abde">

Written for: Claude Code building Huddle over the next 3 days, with you and your professor as reviewers. I've created [SPEC.md](SPEC.md) (665 lines). It's the only file I added; it's untracked and not committed. Summary - Sections are in the order you asked, from Goal through Changelog. There are 8 scenarios, including the hostless night, the AFK player, a phone rejoining mid-game, nights with and without a big screen, the professor's demo, and claiming guest stats later. - Main design decisions: - Each room's live state is one versioned row in Neon, locked while an action is applied, so two simultaneous actions can't overwrite each other. - Each game is a pure module with the same interface. One function builds everything a viewer receives, so secrets can only leave the server one way. - Ably carries only public data, and clients can only subscribe. Secrets travel only in signed-in HTTPS responses, which makes the payload tests simple. - When a deadline passes, whichever phone reports it first triggers processing, and every request also catches up on overdue turns. If every phone has been silent for 2 minutes, the game pauses instead of fast-forwarding. - Drawing strokes go to a separate log, sent in batches every 200 ms and simplified so no point moves more than 1 unit on a 1000-unit canvas. - Team balancing uses multiplayer Elo plus a snake draft with swaps (§4.6). - In test mode, a local realtime channel replaces Ably and fake sign-in replaces Google, so CI needs no secrets. Test mode can't switch on when running on Vercel. - 90 requirements: 84 Must and 6 Should (rate limiting, the recap card, big-screen mode and Most Likely To). - 82 acceptance criteria: 39 Unit, 35 E2E, 6 Deploy and 2 Manual (the playtest and phone install). I checked that every requirement maps to at least one criterion. AC-18 is a dedicated test for the score reset on rejoin. - Phase 1 is a bare app deployed to production before any game is built, so the five deployment risks are proven first. It includes a rough budget of about 110k Ably messages per night. The Ably free limits I quote are from memory, so Phase 1 records the current figures. Open questions (the defaults apply until you change them) 
| # | Question | Default |
|---|---|---|
| Q1 | Season length | Calendar month (IST) |
| Q2 | Does the imposter know they're the imposter? | No; they just get the paired word (a toggle allows it) |
| Q3 | Claim guest stats from another device? | No, same device only |
| Q4 | Do crews need Google sign-in? | No; guests can join, with a nudge to sign in |
| Q5 | Atlas city population threshold | World ≥ 100k, India ≥ 15k |
| Q6 | Does Most Likely To count toward season points? | No |
| Q7 | Can quiz answers be changed before the deadline? | No; the first answer is final |
| Q8 | Spectators and screens per room | 8 and 2 |
| Q9 | Minimum players | 2 for Quiz, Draw and Atlas; 3 for Most Likely To; 4 for Charades and Imposter |
| Q10 | Who confirms a Charades guess? | The actor's tap; the admin can undo |
| Q11 | Reviewing reported questions | No review screen; auto-exclude at 3 reports, plus a CSV export script |
| Q12 | Should the theme follow the phone's setting? | No; always dark until changed |
| Q13 | 24 h room lifetime counted from | Last activity |
Q2 and Q9 change the gameplay most, so they're the ones worth confirming first.

Links: [{"title":"Ably Realtime","url":"https://ably.com/docs/platform/pricing/limits"},{"title":"Ably Realtime","url":"https://ably.com/docs/platform/pricing/free"},{"title":"Pricing built for scale. Billed by the minute.","url":"https://ably.com/pricing"},{"title":"Ably Realtime","url":"https://a…

Ably's Free plan allows about 6 million messages per month, 200 concurrent connections, and 200 concurrent channels. Message size and bandwidth limits are also set, along with some per-second rates.

- **Messages:** The Free plan includes 6,000,000 messages per month and a message rate of 500 per second.
- **Concurrent connections and channels:** Both are capped at 200. Each connection can attach to 200 channels.
- **Message size:** The maximum single published message is 64 KiB on Free.
- **Bandwidth:** Ably's limits table lists a monthly message bandwidth of 28.6 GiB on Free. Message count and bandwidth limits are enforced separately - exceeding one does not affect the other.
- **Other limits:** Each channel is capped at 50 messages per second published. Stored message history on Free is 1 day (per the pricing page), and presence is capped at 200 members per channel.

Note that a third-party comparison page (Ably vs Applozic) describes an older 16 KB free-tier message limit. Ably's own documentation says 64 KiB, so I'd treat 64 KiB as current. Also, Ably's pricing docs say if a user sends (publishes) a message and 10 users receive it (subscribed) that counts as …

| Inbound message rate per connection (per second) | 50 |
| Outbound message rate per connection (per second) | 50 |
| Token TTL limits | Not specified in the page |

Effects are intended to synchronize state between React and external systems such as manually updating the DOM, state management libraries, or other platform APIs. In general, the body of an effect should do one or both of the following:
* Update external systems with the latest state from React.
* Subscribe for updates from some external system, calling setState in a callback function when external state changes.

Calling setState synchronously within an effect body causes cascading renders that can hurt performance, and is not recommended. (https://react.dev/learn/you-might-not-need-an-effect).

}

  /** Report expired deadlines / due bot actions when the server's nextWakeAt passes (SPEC §4.3). */
  private scheduleTick() {
    if (this.tickTimer) clearTimeout(this.tickTimer);
    const wake = this.state.snapshot?.public.nextWakeAt;
    if (wake == null) return;
    const delay = Math.max(0, wake - this.clock.now()) + Math.floor(Math.random() * 300);

export type PublicView = ReturnType<typeof publicView>;

export function nextWakeAt(room: RoomState): number | null {
  if (room.paused) return null;
  const times = [room.phase.deadline, ...room.botPlan.map((b) => b.dueAt)].filter((t): t is number => typeof t === 'number');
  return times.length ? Math.min(...times) : null;
}

Test counts (final run before the Phase 15 commit) - Unit: 38 files, 159 tests, all passed. - E2E: 90 passed. Every spec runs on both Android (Chromium) and iPhone 14 (WebKit) emulation. - Flake check: the E2E suite ran 3 times in a row with no retries: 270 of 270 passed. - Real services (local production build against real Ably and Neon dev): all 6 steps and the drawing probe passed. - AC-80 now plays 3 Quiz questions and a Draw turn on 6 real browsers, with one reload mid-turn, and all end with identical scoreboards. Fixes from Phase 15 The six-browser run against real Neon found a real problem. Every request in a room took the database row lock, even when nothing changed. Phones also estimated the server clock as ahead under load, so they kept checking for timers too early, which added to the queue. As a result, private views arrived about 14 s late and answers missed the question timer. - Lock-free reads: snapshot, tick and heartbeat now read the room without the lock and take it only when something is due. - Timer checks: phones only check a timer once it has certainly passed on the server, and back off after a check that finds nothing due. - Late snapshots: if a newer update overtakes a snapshot, the phone fetches it again. There are new unit tests for both server and clock fixes, and the details are in the PLAN decision log. Two test-only fixes: - WebKit emulation can't hold more than about 5 phones in one browser, so rooms with more phones open extra browsers. - The AC-39 sniffing test now judges "before the reveal" by each frame's own state, not by a timing margin.  * Game data is never cached: rooms always come live from the server. */
const CACHE = 'huddle-shell-v1';
const SHELL = ['/offline', '/manifest.webmanifest', '/icons/icon-192.png', '/icons/icon-512.png', '/icons/apple-touch-icon.png'];

self.addEventListener('install', (event) => {
  event.waitUntil(caches.open(CACHE).then((c) => c.addAll(SHELL)).then(() => self.skipWaiting()));
});

  event.waitUntil(

/** Schedule the next action for each bot seat (demo, R44). */
export function planBots(room: RoomState, ctx: Ctx) {
  room.botPlan = room.botPlan.filter((b) => b.phaseId === room.phase.id);
  const m = gameModule(room);
  if (!m?.bot || room.status !== 'playing' || room.paused) return;
  for (const s of room.seats) {
    if (!s.isBot || s.status !== 'seated') continue;
    if (room.botPlan.some((b) => b.seatId === s.id)) continue;
    const plan = m.bot(room, s, ctx);
    if (plan) room.botPlan.push({ seatId: s.id, dueAt: ctx.now + plan.delayMs, phaseId: room.phase.id, action: plan.action });
  }
}

e4865c7 fix(e2e): pace demo admin actions under the rate limit; split CI into parallel jobs
The fix and the CI split are committed as e4865c7, not pushed. Your server-limit hypothesis was the right one: the MLT demo start was rejected, with HTTP 429 RATE_LIMITED. Root cause: the demo test sent actions faster than the server allows. - The server accepts at most 10 actions per player per second (R46). The demo-games helper sends two actions per game: a start, then End game. - On the CI runner the 11th action, the Most Likely To start, arrived within a second of the first, so the server rejected it. - The demo picker ignored the rejection, so MLT never started and the room moved on to the Night summary. - On my machine each game takes about 250 ms, which stays under the limit. That's why it never failed here. Correction to your summary: the retry didn't fail at helpers.ts:167. Both error-context.md files show the same failure at line 163 (Expected: "mlt", Night summary with 5 games). The retry's trace also shows ten actions returning 200, then a 429 on the 11th, 983 ms after the first. Your other two hypotheses don't hold. A snapshot was fetched after every action, including right after the 429, and every End game returned 200 before the next start. Fix: - Test: the helper counts this page's own actions and, before each start or End game, waits until the 10th most recent one is more than a second old. That waits for the documented limit, so it isn't a blind sleep or a retry. - App: the demo picker now waits for the server's answer, disables its buttons meanwhile, and shows "Too many taps at once. Wait a second and try again." instead of silently doing nothing. Regression tests (in tests/e2e/demo.spec.ts): - Back-to-back: all six demo games started and ended as fast as the server allows, driven directly rather than through slower button clicks. With pacing switched off it fails with exactly CI's error (Expected: "mlt"), so it catches this on any machine. - Rate-limited start: a burst of 10 actions, then a demo tap. The tap must show the error and start no game, and a second tap after the limit window must start MLT. Verification: - Windows: the design spec plus both new tests passed 10× on both devices, 80 of 80, twice. - Linux (WSL): before cleanup, the pacing fix passed the design spec 20 of 20 and the full Android project in CI mode 45 of 45. The picker error and the new tests came after cleanup, so on Linux they're only checked by CI. - Full suite before the commit: 38 unit files / 159 tests, and 94 E2E tests (90 plus the 2 new ones on each device). CI split: .github/workflows/ci.yml now has two jobs. - checks: lint, typecheck and unit tests. - e2e: a matrix for android and iphone, 2 workers each, with a failure on one device not cancelling the other. Each leg installs only its own browser and uploads its own report (playwright-report-android or playwright-report-iphone). Cleanup: - WSL: ~/node24, ~/huddle-ci, ~/pwdebs, ~/pwlibs, the fonts I added in ~/.fonts, and the Playwright browser download I installed (~/.cache/ms-playwright) are all deleted. - Scratchpad: pg16 is deleted. - Leftover processes: my stopped test run had left a test server and its test database running, and I shut them down. - The report: your zip was in Downloads\playwright-report.zip, not C:\projects\huddle-ci-report\. I extracted it into C:\projects\huddle-ci-report\extracted\, and you can delete that folder whenever you like. Two things I couldn't act on: - Your message says the re-run "[passed / failed again]", with the placeholder still in, so I don't know which. Either outcome fits the cause, since it depends on how fast that runner went. - Actions still warns that the v4 actions it uses run on the deprecated Node 20. It's only a warning, so I left them on v4 to keep this change small.

The two suspects have the largest budgets in the suite: 600 s for the demo test, and 900 s for full night with an 800 s playUntil inside it. Full night also starts 7 playUntil loops it doesn't await, and launches its extra WebKit browsers by hand. If the test fails before closeAll, Playwright's teardown never closes those browsers, and the loops keep driving them for up to 800 s. I'll check that against the Linux reproduction when it finishes.

By Playwright's rules a timed-out attempt reports within roughly twice its timeout (the test plus fixture teardown): about 20 minutes for the demo test. Total silence for 35 minutes therefore suggests the whole runner stalled, starving even the Playwright processes, rather than a single wait that never resolves. Software rendering of many animated WebKit pages on 4 vCPUs is a plausible way to get there; the run in progress will show.

37dc613 fix(e2e): bound the long WebKit tests and make CI fail with a report instead of being cancelled
I could find why the job was cancelled with no result, but not the exact trigger of the WebKit stall itself: it never happened in three full iPhone runs on Linux WebKit here. I fixed the parts that turned a stall into a silent cancellation, and CI now fails with a report instead. Committed as 37dc613, not pushed. Which tests: in the iPhone job's 2-worker order, #15 is the solo demo ("every game can be finished alone with real bot play") and the test the other worker started after #20 is #21, the 8-phone full night. Why the job was cancelled without a result: - Budgets far larger than the tests. The demo test had a 600 s timeout, and full night 900 s with 800 s play loops. Each really takes about 3–4 minutes. With CI's one retry on top, a stuck attempt could not report before the 40-minute job limit, and no report was uploaded because the upload only ran on failure. - The demo's play loop wasn't time-bounded. It ran up to 1,200 iterations, each clicking with the default 15 s action timeout. On a stalled WebKit page, where clicks never pass the stability check, every tap burns 15 s. - Full night hand-launched WebKit browsers for phones 5–8. Playwright doesn't own those, so after a failure they stayed alive with 7 unawaited play loops still driving them. What I couldn't confirm: by Playwright's own rules a timed-out test reports within about its timeout plus a 90 s cleanup, so the demo should have shown a failure by about minute 13. Seeing nothing for 35 minutes means the runner itself stopped making progress, and I don't know what caused that on GitHub's machine. - I rebuilt Linux WebKit in WSL (user space only) and ran the exact iPhone job three times: 12 cores, 4 cores, and 4 cores with software rendering like CI. All three passed 47 of 47 in 9.3–9.5 min (#15 about 3.0 min, #21 about 3.7 min). - I did see the same symptom intermittently on Windows WebKit under full-suite load: a visible button never passes the stability check within 15 s. Fixes (WebKit-relevant): - No hand-launched browsers. Phones beyond 4 now reach the same server through 127.0.0.1 or [::1], which WebKit pools separately, so all phones stay in Playwright's own browser and are cleaned up even on failure. - Full night closes its phones in a finally block, with a 420 s timeout and 390 s loops. - The demo test uses the deadline-based playUntil (2 s clicks, 120 s per game, 300 s overall). Fail fast with evidence: - A 25-minute global timeout under the 30-minute step limit and 40-minute job limit. - Trace and screenshot on every failure, video on the CI retry, and the github reporter. - The report is uploaded if: always(). - I proved this with a throwaway never-resolving test: it failed at its timeout with trace, video and screenshot saved, and a short global timeout ended the run with the HTML report written. Things that came up along the way: - Video only on the retry. Recording every page on every run made two WebKit tests flaky under full-suite load. - Three test races fixed. They predate today and only showed up under full-suite load: - AC-55 scanned static JS bundles for the Draw word and matched a random "queue". - AC-42 clicked End game on a Draw that had already ended by itself. - AC-40 tapped ✕ on a leaderboard that had already closed itself on the player's turn. - A tight spot left alone. AC-39 gives the drawer the 4 s test-mode choose window, and it only lost that race with video recording on, so I didn't change the timer. Verification: - Windows: full night, Imposter and the demo tests passed 50 of 50 (5× on both projects). Leaderboard and layout passed 30 of 30, and the screen spec 10 of 10. - Linux WebKit: the full iPhone job passed 47 of 47, plus 15 of 15 repeats of the three heavy specs. - Full suite: the commit rests on the last run, which was fully green (38 unit files / 159 tests, 94 E2E). The run just before it failed Atlas and Imposter on iPhone with that same WebKit stability symptom. Both then passed 10 of 10 under parallel load, so those failures are intermittent; I couldn't reproduce them as a regression. The WSL setup is deleted again, along with the scratchpad scripts and some leftover log files in your WSL home folder. Only your own files are left there. On the next push, if the iPhone job stalls again, it should now end with a timeout failure and an uploaded report (playwright-report-iphone) instead of a cancellation.

Links: [{"title":"Connection Pooling with Vercel Functions","url":"https://examples.vercel.com/guides/connection-pooling-with-functions"},{"title":"connection pooling with functions","url":"https://vercel.com/guides/connection-pooling-with-functions"},{"title":"# Deploy to Vercel (/docs/orm/v6/pris…

The search turned up consistent guidance from Vercel and Prisma docs on `attachDatabasePool`.

- **Purpose:** Vercel's guide says the helper closes idle connections before an instance suspends, which keeps your connection count under control. Prisma's docs describe the same problem: pools on traditional serverless platforms can leak connections when a function is suspended, because they can'…
- **Setup pattern:** Create the pool in the module's global scope, then call `attachDatabasePool(pool)` once, right after creating it. Vercel's examples show this with `pg`. Requests borrow a client and release it in a `finally` block. (Prisma's example passes the same pool to its driver adapter.)
- **Supported clients:** A Vercel knowledge base article says the helper will automatically manage pooling for supported database clients, including PostgresQL (pg), MySQL2, MariaDB, MongoDB, Redis (ioredis), Cassandra (cassandra-driver), and more.
- **Idle timeout tuning:** Vercel's guide suggests a short idle timeout, around 5 seconds, so unused connections close quickly while still allowing reuse under load. It also warns against a max pool size of 1, though the search snippet cut off that advice.

I didn't find details on exactly when suspension happens or how the helper hooks into it internally, so anything beyond the points above would need a look at Vercel's own docs.

The official Neon docs say not to reuse a `Pool` across requests in serverless environments. Node.js is a bit different from Edge.

- **Core rule:** In serverless environments such as Vercel Edge Functions or Cloudflare Workers, WebSocket connections can't outlive a single request. That means Pool or Client objects must be connected, used and closed within a single request handler. The same docs warn against creating them outsi…
- **Node.js setup:** WebSockets aren't built into Node, so you supply a constructor. In Node.js, it takes two lines to configure WebSocket support. The example sets `neonConfig.webSocketConstructor` to the `ws` package. You could replace ws with undici. Another source notes that in Node.js v21 and …
- **Edge-function guidance:** A Neon FAQ says to create the Pool inside the handler, use it, and close it before returning. For Vercel Edge, one guide suggests ctx.waitUntil(pool.end()) so the connection closes without delaying the response.
- **Stateless alternative:** For one-shot queries, prefer the HTTP neon() function, which doesn't have this constraint.
- **Conflicting Vercel guidance:** A PlanetScale page says Vercel Fluid compute reuses warm function instances, making TCP connection pooling safe. It recommends connecting with pg through PgBouncer on port 6432 and pooling connections with attachDatabasePool from @vercel/functions. That is a third…

I didn't find a source that explicitly confirms whether a WebSocket `Pool` can persist across requests on Vercel Node.js functions (non-Edge). The search results don't address that case directly, so treat it as unverified.

● WebFetch https://vercel.com/guides/connection-pooling-with-functions
**Idle timeout:** The guide doesn't name `idleTimeoutMillis`. It recommends a short idle timeout instead: "Use a relatively short idle timeout (e.g., 5 seconds)" and "to ensure unused connections are quickly closed while still enabling reuse during high traffic." Your 5-second value is an example, …

**Max pool size:** The guide advises against a max pool size of 1: "Avoid max pool size of 1: This does not reduce total connections and harms concurrency in Fluid Compute." Instead, it says to "keep the minimum pool size to 1."

**Problem with idle connections during suspension:** Idle timeouts don't fire while an instance is suspended. As the guide puts it, "Idle connection timeouts don't run while suspended" and "connections remain open until either the VM shuts down or the database forcibly closes them." This can produc…

**Fix in the example code:**

```tsx
// Attach the pool to ensure idle connections close before suspension
attachDatabasePool(pool);
```

- On `state` with `v ≤ local.v`: ignore it.
- With `v = local.v + 1`: apply the public view, and fetch a snapshot if the client's own seat is in `privateFor`.
- With `v > local.v + 1`: fetch a snapshot.
- Also fetch a snapshot on first load, on Ably `connected`/`resumed`, on `visibilitychange → visible`, on `focus` and on `online`.
- While visible, send a heartbeat every 25 s. If the reply has `v > local.v`, fetch a snapshot.
- If Ably has not been connected for 10 s, poll the snapshot every 3 s and show a "Reconnecting…" pill until Ably is back.
- Draw catch-up: a gap in stroke `seq`, or a snapshot taken mid-turn, triggers `GET strokes?after=lastSeq`.

  const connectionString = process.env.DATABASE_URL;
  if (!connectionString) throw new Error('Missing environment variable DATABASE_URL');
  // A dead connection must fail instead of hanging a request. connectionTimeoutMillis also bounds waiting for a free
  // pool slot, so it matches the client's 10 s request timeout rather than failing queued work early.
  const opts = { max: 10, connectionTimeoutMillis: 10_000, statement_timeout: 10_000, keepAlive: true };

    // connection can be dead on wake and hang the next query; attachDatabasePool closes idle ones before suspension.
    const p = new pg.Pool({ connectionString, idleTimeoutMillis: 5_000, ...opts });

    return p as unknown as AnyPool;
  }

Production is mostly within budget, but AC-80 failed: requests intermittently stalled for 15–30 s. I've committed a database fix as d3b505c (not pushed). It only reaches production when you push, so AC-80 needs a production rerun after that. Production results (playhuddle.vercel.app, recorded in docs/deploy-checks.md and the PLAN AC table): 
| Check | Result | Budget |
|---|---|---|
| AC-76 CI | Run #3 on 37dc613 green (checks, e2e android, e2e iphone, 10 m 39 s) | ✔ |
| AC-77 action → other phone | p50 847 ms, p95 860 ms over 50 actions | ≤ 1 s ✔ |
| AC-81 stroke delivery (probe) | p50 325 ms, p95 413 ms; 2,324 of 2,324 delivered; 0 errors; 1.33% of the Ably quota per night | ≤ 1 s ✔ |
| AC-78 persistence | room and seat restored in a new browser, first load 2.0 s | ✔ |
| AC-79 Google | redirects to Google with the production callback, no error page | ✔ |
| AC-87 demo | Quiz against bots finished in 89 s | < 2 min ✔ |
| AC-80 six browsers | **fail**: 6 of 9 runs hit a stalled request | ≤ 1 s (action p95 918–920 ms when not stalled) |
AC-78 still needs a repeat across a real redeploy after your push. The probe also logged one Ably token request that took over 10 s (likely a cold start); Ably retried and nothing was lost. The AC-80 failure: - Symptom: a phone sent an answer and got no response for 15 s or more. In other runs a phone couldn't answer for a whole question, or a batch of strokes never arrived. - Cause: on Vercel, the app reused one Neon WebSocket connection pool across requests, with no timeouts. [Neon](https://neon.tech/docs/serverless/serverless-driver?ref=hm) says that pool must not outlive a request in serverless functions. [Vercel](https://vercel.com/guides/connection-pooling-with-functions) says idle timeouts don't run while an instance is suspended, so a pooled connection can be dead when the instance wakes and hang the next query. - Server fix: production now uses pg over TCP to Neon's pooled endpoint, with attachDatabasePool from @vercel/functions, as [Vercel recommends](https://vercel.com/kb/guide/efficiently-manage-database-connection-pools-with-fluid-compute). It also has a 5 s idle timeout and a 30 s limit on getting a connection. - Client fix: catch-up requests now time out after 10 s and actions after 30 s, so one stuck request can no longer freeze a phone. Shorter limits dropped queued actions in the local real-services runs, so I settled on these. - Local proof: against Neon dev and real Ably, the new production branch passes AC-77, AC-78, AC-80, AC-87, the six-browser skeleton and the probe. Two new unit tests cover the timeouts. - Measurement fix: AC-80's 1.6 s stroke figure was an artefact of how the test polled. It now times from the end of each stroke with all viewers checked at once, which gives 1.4 s locally from India. POLISH-1 (R94 / AC-89): - Signed out: a Sign in button sits next to the theme toggle, and the Your crews card says "Sign in to keep your stats on every device". - Signed in: a row under the header shows an initial avatar, your name and Sign out. It's in its own row because it doesn't fit beside the title at 360 px. - Sign out: the phone carries on as a guest, and both prompts come back. - Test: a new E2E test covers both states on both devices. Button-stability check (task 3): I found no infinite or repeating animations. Production is now within the 1 s budget on every latency measure, and the request stalls are gone. AC-80 still fails in its drawing half, for a different reason. I've committed the fix as 42c8598 (not pushed), so it needs your push before I can re-check production. 
| Production (after d3b505c) | p50 | p95 | Budget |
|---|---|---|---|
| Action → other phone (AC-77, 50 actions) | 840 ms | 862 ms | ≤ 1 s ✔ |

The six-browser skeleton converged in 2.7 s, and the probe had 0 errors. AC-78: passes across the redeploy. Room BHRP, created on the previous deployment, is still intact on the new one (version 4, 2 waves, seat "Neha"). The same-deployment check also passed (first load 2.0 s). AC-80 Draw half: failed in all 5 runs that got that far. When a phone reloads mid-drawing, it fetches the strokes so far and then connects to live updates. Strokes drawn during that gap never reached it, and if no later stroke arrives, it never notices anything is missing. 42c8598 fixes this the way SPEC §4.2 already required: the canvas fetches any missing strokes after every snapshot, and the phone refetches a snapshot whenever its live connection restarts. As a bonus, a phone that has fallen back to polling now gets the drawing too. A new regression test fails on the old code and passes on the new. Also in 42c8598: - Test fixes: - AC-87 (demo) had hung on a click with no timeout. It now passes on production in 64 s. - AC-80 now saves its quiz results before the drawing part runs, so a drawing failure can't erase them. - WebKit flakes: tests that only need a word chosen now choose it directly instead of tapping the button, which was intermittently losing a race against the 4-second test-mode timer under load. - Full suite: the commit rests on a green run (39 unit files / 161 tests, 98 E2E). The two runs before it each failed one different iPhone test on that same stability symptom. One was a "Create a room" tap on the static home page, so our animations aren't the cause. Unexplained: two production runs failed while a phone was joining the room, then five runs joined fine. I couldn't reproduce it. To finish AC-80: push 42c8598 and ask me to rerun test:deploy. That's consistent with a stalled runner. Neither Playwright's global timeout nor the step limit fired, and since the step was killed by the job limit, the upload never ran. This is a CI-only change, all in .github/workflows/ci.yml: 1. Sharding: the iPhone E2E becomes 3 matrix jobs (--shard=1/3, 2/3, 3/3) with --workers=1 each. Android is unchanged (1 job, 2 workers). 2. Hard kill: the test command runs under timeout --signal=KILL 20m. timeout only kills its direct child, though. Orphaned browsers, the Next server or Postgres could keep the log pipe open and still hang the step, so after a timeout the step also kills those processes by name. 3. Resource log: a background loop logs uptime and free -m every 60 s, both to the job log, so it's visible even if the runner dies, and to resources.log for the artefact. 4. Upload: with if: always(), uploading playwright-report, test-results and resources.log under a per-job name. Artefact names can't contain "/", so each matrix entry gets a label.

1	# Huddle: Specification (SPEC.md)
2	
3	> Version 0.4 · 2026-10-26 · Status: approved for build (decisions recorded in §11)
4	> Huddle is a party-games web app for Indian friend groups. Everyone plays on their own phone. A laptop or TV can join as an optional display-only big screen.
5	
6	**How to read this document**
7	
8	- **Requirements** use EARS patterns: *Ubiquitous* ("The system shall…"), *Event* ("When…, the system shall…"), *State* ("While…"), *Unwanted* ("If…, then…") and *Optional* ("Where…"). Each one is tagged **Must** or **Should**.
9	- **Acceptance criteria** (AC-n) are pass/fail checks. Each maps to one or more R-numbers and carries one tag:
10	  - **Unit**: Vitest. This covers pure modules and also API handlers run against a local Postgres in CI.
11	  - **E2E**: Playwright with several browser contexts against a local production build (`next build` + `next start`). Every E2E spec runs in two projects: **Chromium with Android phone emulation** and **WebKit with iPhone emulation** (the Safari engine).
12	  - **Deploy**: Playwright or scripted checks against the production Vercel URL. These run after the owner pushes `main`; the builder never deploys.
13	  - **Manual**: a human check. There are only two: the friends playtest and the phone install.
14	- "Active player" means a seated player who is not AFK. "Viewer" means anyone receiving data: a player, a spectator or a big screen.
15	- All times are server times. IST (Asia/Kolkata) is used wherever a calendar date matters.

/** Test mode enables seeded RNG, short timers, the test sign-in provider and the local realtime driver.

  if (process.env.VERCEL_ENV) {
    throw new Error('HUDDLE_TEST_MODE is not allowed on Vercel');

All seven items are done, each committed separately and none pushed. Before every commit the full suite (npm run ci) passed on both Android and iPhone. The SPEC changes are logged as one version, v0.5, with one changelog row, and PLAN has a new Phase 17. I sent the push notification. 
| # | Commit | What the playtest gets |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | 3e5056f | **How-to-play card** before a game's first round: 3 lines plus an example. The game starts when everyone taps "Got it" or after 20 s, and each game shows it only once per room. The admin can switch the cards off in the lobby. |
| 2 | fae77cd | **🎲 Pick for us** adds a game that fits the seated player count (respecting each game's minimum), preferring games not played yet tonight. |
| 3 | fd9010e | **Quick / Normal / Long** on each queued game, with "~N min" and a queue total. The full settings are still under Advanced, which shows "Custom" when edited by hand. |
| 4 | dac5083 | **Share on WhatsApp** button, a large QR code, and "Join as <name>" so joining again is one tap, even after cookies are cleared. |
| 5 | 5a5048e | **Name Place Animal Thing** (cyan). Places are checked against the Atlas database; other answers stand unless most players vote them out. Unique answers score 10, shared ones 5. |
| 6 | 5c53c9a | **Emoji Decode** (lime). 246 puzzles, 71 of them places, with no flag emoji. Alternate place names count (Bombay, Bangalore). |
| 7 | 7ed1a9b | **Two Truths & a Lie** (red, the Should item). Statements and lies stay secret until each reveal. Spotting the lie scores 100; fooling someone scores 50. |
Each new game has demo bots, rejoin and AFK handling, unit tests and E2E on both devices, and is in every cross-game test. No interactive element animates. The last full run passed 234 unit tests and 114/114 E2E. I also screenshotted the new screens at phone width in light and dark mode, and they look right. Things to know before tonight: - Production behaviour change: the How-to-play cards are on for every real room, including the demo. Test mode starts with them off. I updated two deploy checks to match: AC-80 turns the cards off, and the AC-87 demo check taps "Got it". Both only take effect after you push. - A few fixes went into later commits: - Item 1's card had a pop-in animation and an 8 s test-mode timer, which made the iPhone test flaky. It now appears instantly and lasts 20 s; this went in with item 5. - Two Truths treated a missing lie as statement 1; now caught. - "Venice" was dropped because the place database mapped it to Dayton, USA. World cities now carry a country code so this can't recur. - Atlas demo bots now give up more often as the chain grows, so an all-bot Atlas game can't stall the demo. That came from a run where the bots chained 39 places. - Two full runs failed before going green, both iPhone timing failures under machine load: - Item 5's first run: 4 failures; I was running unit tests alongside it. - Item 7's first run: 5 failures, also with a real test bug. The NPAT test picked a 31-character country name, longer than the 30-character answer limit. Each time the failed specs passed when rerun alone, and I reran the full suite before committing. - Longer test: the solo-demo test now plays all nine games, about 6 minutes locally, with a 10-minute limit. That may push the iPhone CI shard that contains it closer to its time budget.

CI is green on the latest commit and production is healthy, but one deploy check needs your decision before it can count as passing reliably. I've stopped there and sent the notification. CI. Your push (7ed1a9b) passed, but one iPhone job spent 22.6 of its 30.7 minutes installing system packages from the runner's slow package mirror. I made three CI-only pushes to fix that: - dc0889c: cut off and retry a stuck install. One shard still failed. - ac8a530: added apt retries, plus public annotations so failures can be read without signing in. Two shards still failed, and the annotations showed why: killing a slow install left apt running and holding its lock, so every retry failed. - 2e15f8b: packages now install once with apt retrying its own downloads and never cut off; the browser download is a separate, cached, retried step. Runs #12 and #13 were fully green, with one shard absorbing a 6-minute slow mirror without failing. The full local suite passed before every commit (234 unit, 114/114 E2E). Two of those runs first failed on full-night's join step on iPhone; it passed alone twice and on the full rerun, the same load stall as before. Production (https://playhuddle.vercel.app) is healthy. Two deploy checks broke because of my How-to-play card, both test-side, and are fixed in dc0889c: - The drawing probe now turns the cards off before starting. - The six-browser wave check had a race that counted 31 waves instead of 30; it now tops up from the server's count once no requests are in flight.

Drawing code hasn't changed, and the server-side probe shows steady delivery. So I didn't revert anything, and I didn't loosen the test. /** Screen cookie = "<roomId>.<token>"; valid only for that room and a token it registered. */
export function isScreenFor(room: RoomState, cookie: string | undefined): boolean {
  if (!cookie) return false;
  const [roomId, token] = cookie.split('.');
  return roomId === room.roomId && Boolean(token) && (room.screens ?? []).includes(token);
